title: Coin Change
description: Brute force to optimized: unmemoized recursive coin exploration versus a bottom-up 1D DP array over amounts.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of coin denominations and a target amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make up exactly that amount (using any denomination any number of times), or -1 if it cannot be made up at all.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","coins array, amount"],["Output","Minimum number of coins summing to exactly amount, or -1"],["Goal","dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a, built from dp[a-coin] for every usable coin denomination"],["Constraints","Up to 12 denominations, amount up to 10^4"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Fewest coins (unlimited supply) to reach an exact target amount\"","The classic unbounded knapsack / coin change 1D DP: dp[a] built from dp[a - coin] for every coin denomination usable at amount a"]]}

blocks.text: Let dp[a] be the fewest coins needed to make up amount a exactly. For each coin denomination that is not larger than a, using that coin means the remaining amount (a minus that coin) needs its own fewest-coins solution, plus this one coin. Taking the minimum over all usable coin denominations gives dp[a]. dp[0] is 0 (no coins needed for amount 0), and any amount that cannot be formed by any combination remains at infinity (later reported as -1).

blocks.title: Analogy: Making Exact Change With the Fewest Bills From an Unlimited Supply
blocks.text: Picture making exact change for a target amount using an unlimited supply of a few bill denominations, wanting to use as FEW bills as possible. The fewest bills for a target amount is 1 (for whichever bill is used) plus the fewest bills for whatever amount remains after using that bill, minimized over every denomination choice.

blocks.caption: dp[a] = 1 + min over every usable coin of dp[a - coin]

blocks.text: Result: -1 (amount 3 cannot be formed using only coins of denomination 2).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: dp[0] = 0, since no coins are needed to make amount 0.

Observation 2: For any amount a greater than 0, using SOME coin c (where c <= a) means the remaining a-c needs its own fewest-coins solution, so this choice costs 1 + dp[a-c].

Observation 3: dp[a] is the MINIMUM of this quantity over every usable coin denomination, since any one of them could be the "last coin used".

Observation 4: If no coin denomination can ever bring an amount down to a validly reachable smaller amount, dp[a] remains at infinity, meaning that amount is unreachable, reported as -1 at the end.
This leads to a bottom-up 1D DP array over amounts from 0 to the target, each entry built from smaller, already-computed amounts.
Recursively try every coin denomination at every remaining amount, without memoization, exploring every possible combination.
Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every coin recursively at every amount directly implements the definition.
This recomputes the same remaining amounts repeatedly across different coin combinations, costing exponential time; a bottom-up DP array computes each amount exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential without memoization, in the worst case.
Space: O(amount) recursion depth.
Limitation: a bottom-up DP array computes dp[a] for every amount from 0 to the target exactly once, reusing already-computed smaller amounts.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a dp array of size amount+1, initialized to infinity (representing "unreachable"), except dp[0] = 0. For each amount a from 1 to the target, for every coin denomination c not exceeding a, update dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a-c] + 1). After filling the entire array, if dp[amount] is still infinity, return -1; otherwise return dp[amount].
Use a bottom-up 1D DP array over amounts, each entry built from smaller amounts via every usable coin denomination.
Dry run for coins = [1, 2, 5], small amounts

blocks.text: Building dp bottom-up from amount 0 upward guarantees that whenever dp[a] is being computed, every dp[a-c] it depends on (for smaller amounts a-c) is already correctly finalized; taking the minimum over every usable coin denomination correctly considers every possible "last coin used", and unreachable amounts naturally stay at infinity, correctly signaling -1 at the end.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(amount times number of coin denominations).
Space: O(amount) for the dp array.

blocks.text: Coin Change is the foundational unbounded knapsack-style 1D DP problem: each amount's answer is built from smaller amounts via every usable coin denomination.

items: Forgetting to initialize dp[0] = 0 correctly, throwing off every later computation.
Using a value like 0 instead of infinity (or a suitably large sentinel) to represent "unreachable", causing incorrect minimum comparisons.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["amount = 0","Returns 0 directly, no coins needed."],["No combination of coins can reach the target amount","Returns -1."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "dp[a] considers every coin as a possible LAST coin used, taking the minimum" clarifies the recurrence and generalizes cleanly to unbounded-supply coin problems.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "fewest coins (unlimited supply) to reach an exact amount", think: a 1D DP array where each amount is built from smaller amounts via every coin denomination.

items: How would you also return ONE actual combination of coins achieving the minimum, not just the count?
Coin Change II (counting combinations rather than minimizing count) and Perfect Squares, both closely related unbounded knapsack DP problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs exponential time in the worst case; the bottom-up DP array costs O(amount times coins), the standard efficient solution.

items: Core Idea: dp[a] = 1 + min over every usable coin c of dp[a-c].
Time: exponential worst case for the brute force, O(amount times coins) for the DP approach.
Space: O(amount) recursion depth for the brute force, O(amount) for the DP approach.
Most Important Observation: every coin denomination is considered as a possible "last coin used" at each amount.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, foundational medium-level DP problem.
One line memory trick: one plus the best remaining amount, over every coin.
